name: Kira Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal day for you on a building site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and do carpentry and general building trades, usually setting timber studs and fitting window frames before the room is closed. My vocational trade certificate taught me the tools, and site years taught me that a wall on a drawing can be straighter than the one in front of us. I like handing a younger worker a level and watching them catch an error. My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, so I value the higher pay this work brings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a form going through the office faster does not change our timber framing. I have never used AI tools and would still measure the stud spacing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have more than six months saved and plenty of local building work, so the mortgage is not threatened by a small software change. I am more concerned with the wrong timber arriving than with the form that ordered it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same framing shifts and mark stud spacing on the wall before the delivery is used. In the first year I would keep checking every window opening against the supplied frame size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and money in this picture. A quicker AI order cannot make an undersized construction window frame fit a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with an undersized frame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the fitting, mark the actual opening and tell the site manager before any trim covers the gap. A neat finish cannot make a poor fit safe or dry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI if the foreman offered it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a small ordering gain. I would give the foreman my measurements on the job sheet and let the office handle its own software.

say: **Faster** office forms do not change timber framing or window fitting.
I would **measure** openings and studs myself.
think: **Higher** pay and more than six months saved make this mild change safe for our mortgage.
The **physical** fit matters more than the ordering screen.
do: **Keep** framing shifts and mark stud spacing on the wall.
**Check** window openings against each supplied frame size.
S0.quote: A quicker AI order cannot make an undersized construction window frame fit a wall.
fieldNote: She **never** uses AI tools and tests each supplied frame against the physical opening.
**Strong** savings and nearby work let her focus on craft quality rather than immediate income fear.

steps.text: Keep framing shifts and mark timber stud spacing on site
Check supplied window frames against actual openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI buying might cut office time, but someone must answer when the wrong window frames come to site. The carpenter cannot fit a short frame by being told the schedule is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering and planning jobs may change first while my hands still build. My own pay looks secure for now, yet software targets could ask the crew to finish walls before replacement frames arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a month of wrong frame deliveries and the paid hours spent waiting. In the first year I would bring the records to the site manager and ask for a named person who can fix the order without marking our crew late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about being blamed for a supplier mistake, not afraid of a screen doing carpentry tomorrow. A building wall does not shrink because an AI buying program chose a smaller window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record for a wrong delivery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note the opening width, delivered frame width, order number and the hour the replacement arrived. That tells the manager exactly why the crew could not finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course to use the buying program?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep measuring on site and send the numbers through the manager. I do not use AI tools, and an office course would not fix the short frame.

say: **AI** buying still needs a named person to correct wrong window orders.
I would **show** real opening sizes to the site manager.
think: **Office** tasks change first, while my carpentry pay looks stable.
**Targets** could blame a crew for time lost on wrong deliveries.
do: **Log** wrong window frames and paid waiting hours for one month.
**Bring** measurements and order numbers to site manager for correction.
feel: **Uneasy** about unfair blame, secure about immediate fitting work.
S1.quote: A building wall does not shrink because an AI buying program chose a smaller window.
fieldNote: She **resists** learning an office tool while supplying exact site measurements.
Her **present** wages seem safe; the concern is schedule pressure and unfair blame from wrong deliveries rather than immediate replacement.

steps.text: Keep carpentry shifts and log wrong frame deliveries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2028 could order and plan the build, with capable robots around 2031 able to frame walls themselves. I would want a site trial on a crooked renovation before a contractor counts fewer workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots take the steady framing hours at forty-eight, our mortgage still needs years of payments and the children are still in school. Strong savings and plenty of nearby site work give us room to look, but neither guarantees the same high wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would gather our mortgage and school costs with my partner and ask the manager when real robot trials are planned. In the first year after 2028, if my paid framing days fall for two months, I would compare written offers from nearby builders before leaving the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing reliable paid days, not overwhelmed. A framing robot that builds a square room has not proved it can fit studs around a bowed construction wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trial would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch it set studs beside a wall that bows and check the spacing with my own tape. A clean new room would not tell me how it handles repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your children’s plans now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep their school spending as it is while my shifts and our savings hold. I would talk to them only if paid days actually changed our family budget.

say: **Thinking** AI may plan by 2028, with capable framing robots around 2031.
I would **ask** for a crooked renovation trial before worker cuts.
think: **Robot** framing could shrink high-paid site days while mortgage and school costs remain.
**Savings** and nearby jobs give options but no wage guarantee.
do: **Review** mortgage and school costs with partner this year.
**Ask** manager when real renovation robot trials are planned.
**Compare** written nearby building offers if framing days fall two months.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, able to search nearby.
S2.quote: A framing robot that builds a square room has not proved it can fit studs around a bowed construction wall.
fieldNote: She **requires** physical proof but does not take a trial as AI learning.
Her **job** search waits for actual lost paid days and written nearby offers.

steps.text: Compare nearby written building offers after two months fewer framing days
Keep framing shifts while pay and family budget hold
Observe crooked-wall robot trial and measure stud spacing before accepting crew cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2031 changes drawings and buying, and capable building robots around 2034 could frame walls. A few years lets builders test those machines on real renovation jobs before claiming the workers are spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-one for the robots, I will still need wages if the mortgage remains. I could check finished framing by hand, but I would not take a lower-paid job just to stand beside a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the contractor this year for written finish-check duties, a paid training course and posted local wages. If the firm funds practical training and a local checking role pays enough for the mortgage and school costs, I would complete the course before 2031 and apply when the post opens; otherwise I would keep framing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the work after 2034, though the longer warning gives me time to compare terms. A construction checker should find the bowed stud with a level before signing a robot’s wall complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a practical course make you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a framed wall at the top and bottom and find a stud that twists under load. Watching a video of a straight wall would not qualify me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is paid but the job is not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay with my framing crew. Paid training alone does not replace a local job that covers our household costs.

say: The **extra** years allow real renovation trials before framing robots reach sites around 2034.
I would **consider** physical finish checking, subject to wages.
think: At **fifty-one** I may still have a mortgage and need comparable pay.
A **lower-paid** role beside a robot would not be a solution.
do: **Request** written finish-check duties, paid course and local wage this year.
**Complete** funded practical course before 2031 if adequate local role posted.
**Apply** for posted checker role if wage covers mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Anxious** about later framing hours, able to compare written terms.
S3.quote: A construction checker should find the bowed stud with a level before signing a robot’s wall complete.
fieldNote: Her **conditional** training concerns physical checking, not adopting AI software.
Course **funding**, a posted local vacancy and pay that covers mortgage and school costs all govern any move from framing.

steps.text: Complete funded practical course before 2031 if adequate local checker job posted
Apply for posted local checker role if pay covers mortgage and school costs
Keep framing shifts until suitable paid offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2036 could change site plans when I am fifty-three, and capable robots around 2039 reach framing when I am fifty-six. A decade gives apprentices time to learn timber work from people who have repaired old buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older and the mortgage may be smaller if pay holds, but that is no promise of a safe job. I could teach practical framing if a real local post pays enough, and I would still expect machines eventually to do hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training manager this year for the assessor course requirements and actual trainer pay. If the contractor funds a practical course on paid time and posts a local trainer role covering household costs, I would complete it before 2036 and apply when it opens, keeping site shifts until an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual machines, with a decent stretch to prepare. An apprentice should learn to spot a bowed construction wall before a robot makes it look straight on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first apprentice lesson be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let them set a level against an old stud wall and mark the bow before cutting timber. A real frame gives a better lesson than a tidy drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a distant trainer role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after my partner and I compare the written wage, travel and school needs. Plenty of jobs are nearby, so I would not move the family for an uncertain teaching post.

say: A **decade** allows paid apprenticeships before framing robots reach sites around 2039.
I would **teach** real wall measurement before machine plans.
think: **Future** family costs might shrink, but no safe role is guaranteed.
A **local** trainer opening must cover household costs.
do: **Request** assessor requirements and trainer pay from manager this year.
**Complete** funded paid-time course before 2036 if suitable local trainer role posted.
**Apply** for posted local trainer role only if wage covers family costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual machines, helped by more preparation time.
S4.quote: An apprentice should learn to spot a bowed construction wall before a robot makes it look straight on a screen.
fieldNote: She **sees** paid teaching as a possible route, not automatic protection from robots.
Her **slower** adoption remains consistent: practical course, real local job and adequate wages come first.

steps.text: Complete funded assessor course before 2036 if suitable local trainer job posted
Apply for posted local trainer role if wage covers household costs
Keep construction shifts until a suitable trainer offer exists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots able to frame walls around 2031 could reduce the high-paid site days that support our mortgage. Real renovation trials and written nearby building offers would help. My tape measure has to answer the bowed wall before a construction robot gets trusted with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will teach apprentices to fit an old building when the easy new walls go to machines. I learned by measuring an opening twice beside another worker. If a contractor wants reliable carpentry, it should pay for that teaching time.

headlineQuote: My tape measure has to answer the bowed wall before a construction robot gets trusted with it.
portrait: **Kira** is a forty-three-year-old construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who frames timber and fits windows on building sites.
**Higher** pay, over six months saved and many nearby building jobs support her partner, two school-age children and mortgage.
She **never** uses AI tools and insists that openings, studs and old walls be measured on site.
**Fast** robots threaten fitting days; longer timelines allow conditional paid finish checking or practical apprentice teaching.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring framing robots around 2031 and reduce high-paid days while mortgage and school costs remain.
whatWouldHelp: **Real** renovation trials and written nearby building offers would help her respond to a pay cut.
